items.title: The Rise of the Sexy-Cozy Autumn Read
items.summary: Unto every season is given a certain kind of book. When the new year beckons a new you, self-help thrives. Breezy beach reads rule the summer. Cookbook recommendations abound in the lead-up to Thanksgiving. Curiously, publishers told me, Easter is big for picture books (which are easy to stick in a basket next to the chocolate bunny). And Halloween is for horror. Time to bust out some Shirley Jackson (or perhaps some Stephen King or Edgar Allan Poe). Yet the days of decorative gourds and darkening evenings have also become a boom season for romance novels—not just any romance novels, but ones targeted at both Halloween and fall more broadly. These books exist on a spectrum of snuggly to spooky: on one end, crispy foliage and adorable bookshops; on the other, the growing subgenre of horror romance . In the middle lie Halloweeny but still-sweet stories of witches brewing love potions, grim reapers falling for guardian angels, and regular old humans getting entangled with creatures of all kinds. This trend results from a brew of ingredients that include market forces, social-media trends, and readers yearning to escape the real world for a cozier one with more regular seasons. Autumnal romances are not an entirely new phenomenon, but they have really taken off in the past two to five years. Winter-holiday-themed romances used to be published around the end of September, according to Leah Hultenschmidt, the publisher of Hachette Book Group’s romance-focused Forever imprint. “People talk about the Christmas creep. But we were really creeping it,” she told me. Now, she said, holiday books are being pushed back because “fall has become its own selling season.” [ Read: The publishing industry’s most swoon-worthy genre ] Taylor Capizola, the general manager of the romance bookstore The Ripped Bodice in Los Angeles, told me that The Ex Hex by Erin Stirling was the first “overtly autumnal, overtly Halloweeny” book she noticed catching on. That book—about a witch who curses her ex-boyfriend—came out in 2021. That same year, Jeannie Chin released the small-town romance novel The Inn on Sweetbriar Lane . It’s set in fall, and features a pumpkin festival. But Chin told me that at the time, she wasn’t thinking of it as a seasonal romance, and her publisher wasn’t really planning to market it that way. ( The cover , with its pink flowers, actually looks pretty spring-y.) “As it came out, I think, is sort of when this ‘fall is the new Christmas’ thing started,” she said. “So we sort of pivoted with the marketing a little bit to take advantage of the fact that it absolutely is a fall book.” Interest has escalated since then. Whereas in the early part of this decade, Capizola might have seen five or so Halloweeny books come into the shop in the fall, by last year The Ripped Bodice was unpacking “boxes and boxes and boxes,” she said. “Just a massive amount.” One of the fall-themed novels that came out this year was Chin’s. With The Cozy Nook Bookshop , “the idea of putting that fall cozy piece front and center was there from the beginning,” Chin said. This time, it has pumpkins on the cover. To be fair to fall , it is very romantic. The leaves, the chill, the steamy beverages, and the beckoning of the fireplace all set the mood for what many hopeful singles call “cuffing season.” The beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail famously takes place in fall, with Tom Hanks rhapsodizing about “a bouquet of newly sharpened pencils”—a quote that makes the rounds on social media every autumn. But there’s romance set in the fall, and then there’s fall romance. “We are giving them something seasonal on purpose,” Hultenschmidt said of her publishing imprint. And seasonal romances can be very on the nose. Take Emily Henry’s 2020 romance, a beach read titled Beach Read , that is set at a lakeside beach town and stars an author who writes beach reads. Cindy Hwang, the editorial director at Berkley, which publishes Henry, told me she thinks that the popularity of Beach Read helped launch the trend of highly literal seasonal romances. Some of these fall books practically grab you by the collar, shove a pointy hat on your head, and pour a pumpkin-spice latte down your throat. For instance, last September, Amazon published a collection of short stories for Kindle and audiobook called Scared Sexy , one of which is about a sexy sleep-paralysis demon. All of the stories feature creatures, and most mention Halloween in some way. A couple of these stories were among Kindle’s most-purchased romance books of 2025, according to the blog Romancing the Data , which tracks romance best sellers. For the same reason someone might watch scary movies or carve a pumpkin, they pick up sexy Halloween books to get into the spirit of the season. But why is seasonality something readers are particularly craving now ? It may partly follow from the rise of “spooky season” as a concept. The phrase doesn’t seem to have been used much before 2018 or so, according to Google Trends . It’s invoked as a way of extending the playfully scary energy of Halloween throughout the fall, and giving adults an excuse to partake in seasonal delights along with kids. Hultenschmidt suggested that the whole snuggly-to-spooky spectrum could be explained by the sense of uncertainty and instability pervading the culture right now. In the face of economic anxiety and political tension, people may seek safety in the comfort of a romance novel and its guaranteed happily-ever-after. Or “they want the terror of a horror novel to be like ‘Oh, well thank God it’s not this bad,’” she said. This might also explain the appeal of hybrid horror-romance books like this year’s Kiss Slay Replay by Rachel Harrison, about a woman trapped in a time loop at her best friend’s wedding, with a masked killer on the rampage and a handsome wedding guest to help her fight back. [ Read: The dark reality behind ‘cozy mysteries’ ] I also wonder if some of the appeal is a result of climate change. Seasons other than summer are getting shorter , and all seasons are becoming more unpredictable . When I spoke with Hwang earlier this month, the high in our respective East Coast cities (D.C. and New York) was nearly 80 degrees. If I wanted to catch that classic fall feeling in mid-October this year, I would’ve been better served by cracking open a book than by going outside. In addition to the comfort and the spookiness, all of the attention on fall stems from one more thing: marketing. Romance and autumn may go together these days like apple cider and cinnamon sticks, but that’s in part because each is having a moment that businesses have seized on. Retailers have greatly expanded their lines of fall-coded decor, food, candles, and more. Cozy as a marketing aesthetic caught on during the pandemic and never quite left. Seasonal swag is a built-in yearly sales opportunity, no less so in publishing than in any other business. At the same time, romance has become so successful that it could be said to be propping up the entire publishing industry. The genre is also a particularly fast-paced business. Many romance readers read a lot —Capizola told me some of her customers can read two novels in a day—and romance writers oblige their fans’ appetites with a regular supply of new books. Take Christina Lauren, the pen name of two best friends who co-write their books. Some years they have released two or even three full-length novels. This pace may make it easier to jump on trends relatively quickly, compared with genres where longer lead times are the standard. “Romance as a genre is currently driven in many ways by online trends,” Jamie Fortin, the founder of Friends to Lovers bookstore in Alexandria, Virginia, told me. (The exploding category of romantasy —romance plus fantasy— owes a lot to social-media hype , as well.) [ Read: The fan-fiction friendship that fueled a romance-novel empire ] It certainly helps that a seasonal read lends itself well to social media. TikTok and Insta

items.title: Stop trying to find yourself
items.summary: Philosopher Joe Folley is skeptical that there’s a core self down there to find. In this Big Think Conversation with Jonny Thomson, he makes the case for a self that gets built rather than excavated — and argues that the attention it takes to build one has been quietly thinned down into something you spend, trade, and optimize. Then: why nearly everyone reads the wrong Camus book, and why Camus himself seems to have thought his most famous philosophy was only half finished. Joe Folley holds an undergraduate degree and a master’s in philosophy from Cambridge and is the creator of the YouTube channel Unsolicited Advice, where he makes philosophy accessible to a broad audience. This video Stop trying to find yourself is featured on Big Think .

items.title: The Power of Touch in High Art
items.summary: Don’t Touch the Art by DS Waldman The first time I brought my mother to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, she reached out and touched one of my favorite paintings. I’d acquired a long-term press pass to the museum to help finish my first book, which features a number of ekphrastic poems and art criticism, so for two years I came and went for free. Having spent considerable time there, I was excited to show my mother, an old-process photographer, some of my favorite things, especially in the cameraless photography wing. Together, and separately, we drifted around the gallery, along walls of Man Ray’s ghostly rayographs, Allison Rossiter’s experimental photograms printed on expired, thus unstable, photo paper. At the gallery’s exit—or entrance, depending on one’s path—there hung a wall-size grid of cyanotypic squares, all together forming a single, very large blue rectangle. Across the blue grid, sprays and roils of white, like sea foam, as though an actual wave had broken across the wall, had broken but frozen mid-break. I could almost taste the marine brine, feel the coastal chill. The piece was titled Littoral Drift Nearshore #209, the artist Meghan Riepenhoff. And I’d learned from the wall placard that Riepenhoff did, in fact, incorporate seawater into the work, throwing buckets of water and silt from Washington’s Fletcher Bay across the cyan-exposed paper. I remember looking across the gallery and watching my mother see Littoral Drift for the first time, thrilling a little to share the experience of it with her, eager to hear what she thought. She stood, first, at a distance, taking in the whole of the composition, then she walked slowly toward it. I expected her to stop at some middle distance, or maybe at a very near point, inspecting the granular detail of the thing. But she didn’t stop. I watched my mother walk right up to the piece and lift a corner of one of the blue squares off the wall, inspecting the backside of the paper. The experience did open in me a fundamental conundrum around how we, collectively, are allowed to experience art. I don’t know how the attendant hadn’t stopped her—they stood only a few yards away. When they came to and saw my mother with the art in her hand, they shouted very loudly, told her to back away, then approached and told her that if it happened again, they’d have to ask her to leave. My mother and I left the gallery and regrouped in the atrium. “I’m so embarrassed,” she said, genuine surprise on her face, “I don’t know what got into me.” She said she’d felt like a child, had felt and given in to that infant impulse to reach out and touch. My mother loves the ocean, and living in landlocked Kentucky, she doesn’t get to see it—or touch it—very often. We’ve gone together to many art museums, domestic and abroad; I’ve never seen her do anything like that, touching the art. And I found myself, for the rest of our afternoon at SFMOMA, privately upset with the attendant who had so publicly scolded my mother, embarrassed her, sent her—for the rest of the afternoon—a little farther into herself, and away from the art. My mother stayed well behind the tape lines on the floor, kept her hands behind her back. Of course, I don’t blame the attendant for doing their job, and I also don’t believe anyone at any time, in a museum, should be allowed to put their hands on a piece of art. We protect and preserve these things so we and future generations can continue experiencing them, so they remain actual, so Littoral Drift Nearshore #209 , in 10 years, 50, won’t become a ghost we know only from photographs. But the experience did open in me a fundamental conundrum around how we, collectively, are allowed to experience art. There’s the familiar criticism of high art, that because of the often exorbitant cost of museum tickets, and the general concentration of the “best” museums in expensive cities like San Francisco and New York and Paris and London, high art is in effect only available to those that can afford the experience—an increasingly smaller and smaller demographic. And even then, with the ticket purchased, the traditional museum experience is almost uncomfortably formal, sterile, the space between the viewer and object charged with the tension of surveillance, the boundaries demarked with tape and ropes and sometimes plates of glass, the eyes of guards and ceiling cameras watching you look at the mural or sculpture, watching you watch the video installation. A former teacher of mine, a poet and art lover, told me she disliked art museums because they made her feel constipated. I don’t especially mind the traditional museum experience, or maybe I’ve just grown accustomed to it. I can’t easily imagine an alternative, a way of being around high art that feels less stiff while also protecting and preserving the art objects. It seems something would have to give. I’m reminded of a scene in Garth Greenwell’s novel Cleanness in which the narrator, an American living and teaching in Bulgaria, goes out drinking one night with a group of former students. They gather with their bottles of vodka and cartons of orange juice in a sort of public park or square adorned with a number of marble pillars and cornices, all from antiquity, all in some stage of decay or brokenness. The narrator has a visceral reaction when his former student sets the orange juice carton on top of one of these ancient pillars, using it as a table. But the student pushes back, “ . . . you’re still such an American,” he teases, “we have stuff like this everywhere.” The ancient art existed simply as part of the cityscape; it was there for anyone to touch or sit on or use as a table for their booze. There’s something undeniably democratic about it, the art or artifact made as common and available as a public water fountain or a bench in a park. It makes me want to read that word “American,” in the scene, as “capitalist.” Whereas the pillar beneath the orange juice has more or less been freed from capital—returned to the people—so much high art, like Littoral Drift, and high archaeology, as we might see in the Egyptian Art Wing of the Met, exists behind the glass plate of money, markets, and valuation. Behind the wonder, or next to it, the specter of capital colored almost everything. My senior year in college, our Art History thesis cohort took a trip to New York, where our instructor, through some friend of a friend, managed to coordinate a private tour of the Met’s painting conservation department. We arrived early to the museum, before it opened, and were escorted through a back entrance to the conservation studios, which I’d expected to look like a sterile, windowless laboratory, all the conservationists in hazmat suits. But the space was gorgeous, warm, with floor-to-ceiling windows on one side, wood tables and stools and easels, the space in reality more like an actual artists’ studio, as though the Rembrandts and O’Keefes had been created there, not just restored. Our guide, Sarah, brought us into the studio and showed us a painting she’d just begun working on, a Renaissance fresco that had been removed from its frame and set across several easels. She walked us through her process, how she removed discolored varnish and old overpaints, how she retouched areas where paint had flaked away, how she “ingilded” abrasions. These people are artists, I thought, listening to Sarah, who wore a smock and magnifying lens and told us about the rates of degradation for different paints. She looked with what seemed authentic wonder at the fresco, a wonder similar, maybe, to mine and my cohort-mates’. But behind the wonder, or next to it, the specter of capital colored almost everything Sarah said. The fresco was in excellent condition, she told us, for a piece its age,

items.title: Was dark matter first discovered by Fritz Zwicky or Vera Rubin?
items.summary: It’s hard to believe, but the idea that the Universe was dominated not by normal matter but rather by dark matter — a novel form of non-interacting matter that’s completely distinct from protons, neutrons, and electrons — goes all the way back to 1933: nearly a full century ago. For decades, the overwhelming majority of the leading astronomers and physicists dismissed the idea as being ill-motivated and lacking sufficient evidence backing it, and it gained very little traction on both the theoretical and observational fronts throughout the 1930s, 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s. It was only with the novel results and improved instrumentation initially leveraged by Vera Rubin and Kent Ford, and then further developed by Rubin on her own, that dark matter was brought into the cosmological mainstream in 1969 and then throughout the 1970s. So who should get the credit for discovering dark matter? Did either Fritz Zwicky, who first presented that initial 1933 evidence and even coined the term dunkle materie , which directly translates to dark matter, or Vera Rubin, with her pioneering work concerning galactic rotation in the 1970s, actually discover dark matter? Could either of them be credited with at least presenting the overwhelming evidence in favor of dark matter’s existence? Or is it unfair to say that dark matter was actually discovered by either of them, including up through and including the present day? Although the astronomical evidence is overwhelming for dark matter’s existence , attributing dark matter’s “discovery” to any one individual misses the entire point of science, including how it’s conducted and how conclusions are reached. Here’s a context-rich history of dark matter that might surprise you in many ways. The Hooker Telescope: the largest and most powerful telescope in the world from 1917–1949. This telescope was 100 inches (2.54 meters) in diameter, making it larger than the primary mirror on the Hubble Space Telescope today. It held the crown for largest telescope in the world until the Hale telescope, double the diameter of this one, was finally completed in 1949, 21 years after work was begun on it. This was the one telescope, more than any other, that was the key to unlocking the expanding Universe. Credit : H. Armstrong Roberts/ClassicStock By the time the 1930s came along, even though that was already a full 93 years ago, astronomy was actually quite advanced as a science. Telescope apertures had already reached 100 inches (2.54 meters, which is larger than the Hubble Space Telescope’s mirror) and a 200-inch (5.1 meter) telescope — double the diameter and with four times the light-gathering power — was already under construction. We had learned that the spiral and elliptical nebulae in the sky were actually galaxies unto themselves, with their own stars and matter inside, located millions of light-years beyond the Milky Way. We knew the properties of stars and how brightness, mass, color/temperature, and ionization were all related. We knew that the Universe was expanding, with light from more distant galaxies appearing systematically redshifted directly dependent on their distance from us. On top of that, we had even measured the expansion rate: the first determination of what we now know as the Hubble constant . It was with this picture of the cosmos that the first hints of dark matter were discovered. In 1933, Fritz Zwicky was studying the galaxies in the Coma Cluster : a cluster of galaxies located just ~300 million light-years away. With over 1,000 identified galaxies in it today, it’s larger, richer, and more regular than the nearby Virgo Cluster (itself only ~50–60 million light-years away), and many of its galaxies are large, bright, and luminous. The Coma Cluster of galaxies, as seen with a composite of modern space and ground-based telescopes. The infrared data comes from the Spitzer Space Telescope, while ground-based data comes from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The Coma Cluster is dominated by two giant elliptical galaxies, with over 1000 other spirals and ellipticals inside. Gas-free, red-and-dead elliptical galaxies are very common, especially toward the cluster center, in large galaxy clusters such as this one. The speed of galaxies within the cluster can be used to help determine the cluster’s total mass, revealing our first evidence for dark matter in the 1930s. Credit : NASA / JPL-Caltech / L. Jenkins (GSFC) Even with the instruments available to Zwicky at the time, he was able to identify dozens of individual member galaxies of the Coma Cluster, including a number of bright spirals (mostly toward the cluster’s outskirts) and giant ellipticals (mostly toward the cluster’s center). These individual galaxies all have approximately the same redshift, because at around 320 million light-years away, the entire cluster is receding from us along with the expanding Universe. When he took the average redshift of the galaxies in the cluster, he got a value that corresponded to a speed of just about 2% the speed of light. The cluster was definitely speeding away from us along with the expansion of the Universe. But Zwicky didn’t have to settle for the average value of the redshift across many different galaxies; he was able to measure the redshift of each member galaxy that he could resolve individually. Some of them — maybe even most of them — were moving with either the average value or a value close to the average, as indicated by their redshift. But others possessed redshift values that were much higher or much lower than the average, indicating that these galaxies making up the cluster were zipping around incredibly fast inside. It was as though the individual galaxies were swarming, like a hive of bees, around and through the galaxy cluster itself. In order for that configuration to be a stable one, there had to be an enormous amount of mass holding this galaxy cluster together: with enough gravity to keep these fast-moving galaxies from escaping from the cluster’s overall gravitational pull. Since there was no evidence that this cluster (or any similar cluster) of galaxies was flying apart, that mass must be present, even if we couldn’t see it. The velocities of the galaxies in the Coma Cluster, from which the total mass of the cluster can be inferred to keep it gravitationally bound. Note that this data, taken more than 50 years after Zwicky’s initial contentions, matches almost perfectly with what Zwicky himself contended way back in 1933: that far more mass must be present than stars, gas, plasma, dust, black holes, and all other forms of normal matter combined can account for. Credit : G. Gavazzi, Astrophysical Journal, 1987 Zwicky’s reasoning proceeded as follows: as astronomers, we know how stars work, and if we measure the starlight from all the galaxies in the cluster that we see, we can determine how much mass is in these galaxies and in the whole cluster, we also know how gravity and the expanding Universe works, so if we measure the average redshift of the cluster, we know how far away it is, and based on how fast we see these galaxies moving, there must be at least a certain amount of mass in there due to gravity. When he compared the “mass from starlight” number with the “mass from gravitation” number, he realized that the latter number was over 400 times larger than the first number. Even if there were a small, unidentified error somewhere, he argued, this was an incredibly high magnitude of a mismatch, and no small error could account for all of it. Therefore, as a necessity, there must be much more matter out there than the normal matter that we knew of could account for. He called this unseen matter dunkle materie : directly translated as dark matter. Zwicky was quite a gifted astronomer, but also an iconoclast who was known for agitating the mainstream.
